name: CurbClock: a curb witness and 5-minute wait clock for paratransit riders
track: Ring (primary). Can also enter the AWS Builder and Open Source mini challenges.
pitch: A Ring camera that can see the curb acts as the rider's own witness. When a vehicle stops during the paratransit pickup window, CurbClock starts the agency's 5-minute wait clock on the rider's accessible screen and pages a named helper, who has to accept. If the vehicle leaves early, it builds a dated dispute packet that quotes the agency's own no-show rule. It records observations only. It never gives a verdict, and it never claims who was in the vehicle.
primary_user: ADA paratransit riders with mobility or vision disabilities who are picked up curb-to-curb from a house or duplex where a Ring doorbell or camera can see the curb. Secondary users are one or two named helpers (a family caregiver or personal care attendant) who help the rider reach the vehicle. In practice this is US-only, because both ADA paratransit and the Ring partner path are US.
original_mechanism: Policy-as-code dwell evaluation. Three inputs are fused into a vehicle-present interval with explicit uncertainty: (1) the rider's scheduled pickup; (2) a machine-readable version of that agency's published no-show policy (window anchor and length, wait minutes, early-arrival rule, dispute deadline, agency-error clauses, each with its quoted source text); (3) Ring observations. Those observations are a vehicle event that wakes the pipeline, then WHEP frames sampled through chained 60 s sessions, classified by an object detector (car/bus/truck classes) inside a curb polygon. The watermark band and privacy zones are masked, and an enter/exit hysteresis is applied. The interval drives an accessible countdown and a named-helper accept ladder (primary, then backup, with timeouts). On a missed trip, a pure evaluator checks the interval against the agency's own error clauses and emits 'candidate agency-error: departed 2:50 before the 5-minute wait'. It never says who was in the vehicle or whether the rider was at fault. On a real device with a plan, the window clip is downloaded afterwards and the interval is recomputed offline. Each packet records whether it came from live samples or from the clip.
removal_test: Without Ring, what is left is a countdown timer plus the agency's own tracking app, which is the status quo. Both the 'a vehicle is at your curb now' trigger and the rider's own arrival/departure record disappear, and those are the product. Ring is load-bearing. Honest caveat: any curb-facing camera with a partner API could play this role. The indispensability comes from Ring being the camera already mounted at the door, not from a capability only Ring has.
wow_moment_45s: 0-8 s: The rider's tablet shows today's trip: dialysis, pickup 2:00-2:30, driver waits 5 min, per the Union City policy (clause quoted on tap). 8-22 s, REAL: Ring Playground live view of the simulated Vehicle event, with the CC BY attribution on screen. The in-browser detector boxes a vehicle inside the curb zone. The rider's screen flips to a large 'Vehicle at your curb 2:07 - 5:00' countdown with sound, and the helper's phone shows 'Asha needs help to the curb - Accept?'. The helper taps Accept. 22-40 s, SIMULATED (ring-sandbox emulator, labelled on screen, team-recorded curb footage): the vehicle leaves at 2:09:10. CurbClock shows that the vehicle left after 2 min 10 s, while the agency's policy lists departing without the 5-minute wait as an agency error. One tap produces a dispute packet with timeline, two watermarked frames (people blurred), the quoted clause and 'dispute by Fri 5 pm'.

It observes the vehicle at this curb, runs the 5-minute clock against the agency's own rule, pages a helper, and produces a dispute packet. Whether 'Where's My Ride' exposes arrival or wait logs to riders is not verified in reviewed sources.

rivals.name: Ring Smart Alerts (vehicle detection)
rivals.our_difference: A vehicle alert carries no pickup window, no wait clock, no helper acceptance and no policy-based dispute packet. Dwell measurement in native alerts is not verified in reviewed sources.

rivals.name: School Bus Home (Ring Appstore)
rivals.our_difference: Built for paratransit rules (window anchors, 5-minute wait, agency-error clauses, dispute deadlines), accessible rider output and helper acceptance. Shows the expected-window pattern is already shipped for one niche.

mvp_scope: Playground token flow and device/status/capabilities reads. Every screen shows a REAL badge for live Ring calls and a SIMULATED badge for emulator events.

Curb-watcher browser tab. A server-proxied WHEP session (SDP exchange server-side, since CORS blocks browser calls to Ring) is re-negotiated within the 60 s cap. MediaPipe object detector runs in the browser on frames, inside a rider-drawn curb polygon, with the watermark band masked. Output is vehicle-present intervals with hysteresis. Raw frames never leave the browser.

ring-sandbox 0.5.0 emulator sends HMAC-signed motion_detected sub_type=vehicle webhooks. Four scenario YAMLs run on team-recorded curb footage served as snapshots: boarded on time, left before 5 min, arrived before window, no vehicle in window.
Trip and policy model seeded with Union City, Access Services LA and Erie LIFT parameters. Each field links to its quoted source clause.
Wait clock and named-helper accept ladder (primary, then backup, 60 s timeout), on an accessible rider PWA: large type, high contrast, screen-reader labels, audible cue, WCAG 2.2 AA target.

Closure: the rider or helper taps Boarded or Missed. On Missed, the evaluator builds a dispute packet (PDF): timeline, at most 3 watermarked frames with people blurred, quoted clause, deadline, free-text rider statement. Packets auto-delete 30 days after the dispute deadline.
AWS deployment in us-east-1, plus unit tests for the evaluator, HMAC verification over raw bytes and dedupe on meta.request_id. README includes a verified-vs-simulated table and a friction log.
hardware: Development on the MacBook M4 Pro (24 GB); headless Chromium for WHEP capture and tests. Two phones of any make for the rider and helper PWAs. A smartphone to record consented curb footage for simulated scenarios (team's own street; people blurred, no plates kept). No Ring hardware is needed for the Playground path. Optional: a US-located Ring camera that sees the curb, with a Ring plan (conditional real path).

estimate.cloud_cost_usd: Estimate: about $3-15 total through 20 Nov 2026. Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB on-demand and EventBridge Scheduler stay inside listed free allowances at demo volume (Lambda 1M requests and 400k GB-s/month; Scheduler 14M invocations/month), if the account's plan includes them. CloudWatch logs and S3 cost a few dollars. Optional Nova Lite at $0.06/$0.24 per 1M input/output tokens (Ohio rates; us-east-1 assumed equal) comes to under $1 for about 1,000 calls. Vision runs in the browser, so inference costs nothing. Firecrawl API credits for a few dozen extractions are not priced here.
estimate.assumptions: These are estimates, not measurements. One engineer comfortable with Python/TypeScript and basic WebRTC. Hours include day-1 validation spikes (8h), WHEP capture (8h), detector and dwell tracker (10h), emulator scenarios and footage (8h), policy model and evaluator (8h), Firecrawl onboarding (5h), wait clock and helper ladder (8h), accessible PWAs (14h), dispute packet (7h), AWS deployment (8h), tests (6h), and video, README, friction log and feedback (12h). hours_duo is elapsed hours per person when split across two people, including about 15% coordination overhead. 20 calendar days remain; internal target 22 Oct.

blockers: WHEP from the Playground has conflicting reports (frames captured 2026-09-23 with headless Chrome only; a failure reported 2026-09-30). Reproduce on day 1.
Content of the Playground Vehicle footage is unknown. It may not show a curb or a van.
The Playground has no vehicle webhooks or sub_type, so the event layer for an India team must be simulated and labelled.
The real path needs a US device, Ring plan, identity-verified developer account and account linking, none of which the team has confirmed.
Bedrock quota may be 0 on a new account (forum reports). The core does not depend on Bedrock.
Node v25 on the machine versus the starter's Next.js 14 (use nvm).
fallback: If WHEP fails: run the CV on ring-sandbox snapshots of team footage (labelled SIMULATED), keep real Playground device/status/history reads as the live Ring calls, and document the failure in the friction log. If vehicle CV is unreliable on watermarked frames: drive dwell from simulated motion.vehicle start/end plus one-tap rider or helper confirmation. If the dispute angle is falsified: ship the readiness and helper loop alone, and present the packet as a personal log.
judge_rejection_risks: For an India-based team, most of the event layer is simulated. Only device reads, history and Playground live view are real.
Many doorbells cannot see the curb, and apartment riders are excluded, so the addressable share of riders is unproven.
A camera cannot prove the vehicle was the paratransit van, that the driver tried to locate the rider, or that the rider was ready. Judges may see the evidence as weak.
Whether agencies accept rider-held evidence was not verified.
It may be read as a 'vehicle alert' (the Obvious category) if the policy and dispute mechanics are not shown clearly in the video.
Narrow, US-only population.
Recording a public street captures drivers and passers-by. Mitigated by blurring people and keeping no plates, but still sensitive.
risk_profile: Medium-high technical and simulation risk (vehicle CV on pre-recorded watermarked footage; event layer simulated). High problem severity backed by primary-source policies. Medium adoption risk (agency acceptance of rider evidence unverified). Low platform-policy risk as long as there is no OCR, face or plate analysis.
aws_builder_path: API Gateway HTTP API and a Python Lambda verify Ring's HMAC on raw bytes and ack within Ring's 5 s limit, then SQS, a worker Lambda and DynamoDB (trips, observations, policies). EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedules hold the 5-minute clock, helper timeouts and dispute-deadline reminders, so timers survive restarts; the pricing page lists 14M Scheduler invocations/month free. S3 with lifecycle rules holds packets that expire. An optional Bedrock Nova Lite call rewrites the fixed letter template in plain language; all decisions stay deterministic. AWS Budgets alarm. Built with Kiro or Claude Code on Bedrock (forum 45321 says this counts). The value is durable timers and a reliable public webhook endpoint, not a logo.
open_source_path: (1) Publish 'paratransit-noshow-policies' (MIT code, CC BY data): a JSON schema plus a dataset of agency policies with source URLs, quoted clauses and retrieval dates, and a pure evaluate_pickup(observations, policy) function with table-driven tests. (2) Upstream PR to ring-sandbox adding vehicle-dwell scenarios (early_departure, before_window, no_vehicle) and a --media-dir example; its README names scenario files as the most valuable contribution. (3) Publish the headless-Chrome WHEP frame-capture script with its failure modes. One entrant reports a werift offer got HTTP 500 and only headless Chrome worked.

conditions: The Playground opens for the user's Amazon Developer account from India (regional gating unverified).

strongest_rival.rival: ProofClock, together with School Bus Home (both from the same developer, erbacciltd, on the Ring Appstore)
strongest_rival.why: ProofClock already ships CurbClock's 'original mechanism' in general form. From Ring motion timestamps alone, it records when someone arrived, how long they stayed and whether they met the window. It issues a verdict (Verified, Short, No-show or Unverifiable) and exports a monthly CSV 'for billing and SLA disputes'. Its sibling School Bus Home (https://ring.com/appstore/school-bus-home) adds the rest: an expected window at entry cameras, vehicle-class detection (a US yellow school bus), a confirming still kept 31 days, and a 'no bus by expected time' heads-up. Combined, the two cover about 70% of CurbClock: window, vehicle at the entrance, dwell, verdict, dispute export and a kept frame. That share is my estimate. TAKE makes the overlap worse. TAKE is becoming the default encryption for all Ring customers, and during rollout partner apps cannot read clips or snapshots or open live streams on TAKE devices (developer FAQ Q10). On real devices CurbClock's CV path therefore degrades to metadata-only dwell, which is exactly ProofClock's design. What no reviewed rival offers: paratransit rule clauses (early-arrival anchor, 5-minute wait, dispute deadline), a live countdown for the rider, helper acceptance with escalation, and an agency-specific dispute letter.

redteam_round1.differentiation_holds:
Partially. It is not a latent-LLM idea: the core is a deterministic policy evaluator, timers and CV, and the LLM pieces (Nova letter rephrasing, Firecrawl JSON extraction) are optional and should be cut. It does not collapse completely either. Among the 56 Ring Appstore listings, the roughly 36 visible hackathon Ring repos and the agency apps reviewed, none combines paratransit no-show rule clauses, a policy-anchored wait clock shown to the rider, named-helper acceptance with escalation, and an agency-specific dispute letter with a deadline. The domain is also uncrowded in the hackathon field.

Each component taken alone is not new:
- Vehicle-arrival alerting is native (Ring Smart Alerts, Video Descriptions with Alexa, Shared Users) and agency-provided (Valley Metro arrival notification, Pace TripCheck imminent-arrival alert, dispatcher calls per DREDF).
- The window-plus-vehicle-plus-kept-evidence pattern is School Bus Home.
- The arrival-plus-dwell-plus-window-plus-verdict-plus-dispute-export evaluator is ProofClock.

The concept's originality claim of 4 is overstated. What is defensible is the paratransit-specific workflow layer, not the 'policy-as-code dwell evaluation' mechanism. The 'Ring as independent witness' thesis is weakened by TAKE, by the inability to identify the vehicle, and by agency acceptance being unverified.
redteam_round1.redesign:
Narrow it to 'CurbClock: a human-confirmed, policy-anchored pickup log'. Drop CV-as-witness as the thesis.

(1) Trigger and identification. A vehicle event opens a 60 s Ring live view on the helper's phone through a server-proxied WHEP exchange with a browser-built offer. The vehicle event is a motion_detected sub_type=vehicle webhook: labelled SIMULATED in the demo, real only on US devices. The rider can also tap 'my ride should be here' to open the same view. Live view is REAL on the Playground. The in-browser detector box is only a hint. The helper, or a sighted rider, answers 'Is this your ride? Yes / No / Can't tell', and only 'Yes' starts the clock. This replaces unverifiable CV identification with a human confirmation backed by a watermarked Ring frame and the on_demand history entry Ring logs for that session (REAL, readable on the Playground per doorstep-ring and forum 45309). It also makes the Playground calls load-bearing even if the Vehicle footage turns out to be generic.

(2) Clock. Fully model ONE agency policy (Union City or Access Services LA), including the early-arrival rule that starts the 5 minutes at the scheduled time. Include two more agency policies as schema data only. EventBridge Scheduler holds the clock and the helper ladder (primary, then backup, 60 s timeout). The rider PWA speaks the countdown and shows it in large type (WCAG 2.2 AA).

(3) Departure. A second live check, or the vehicle-event end (SIMULATED), confirmed by the helper.

(4) Output. Reframe the dispute packet as an 'AVL review request'. It is a one-page letter that quotes the agency's own clause, gives the rider-side timeline (helper-confirmed arrival and departure, Ring live-view session IDs and history timestamps) and at most 2 watermarked frames. It asks the agency to check its own AVL/MDT records for that trip before the dispute deadline. It never claims proof, and never claims the agency accepts rider video.

(5) Cut Firecrawl onboarding, Bedrock, SQS, multi-agency extraction and the offline clip recompute. Keep API Gateway + Lambda (HMAC over raw bytes, 2xx under 5 s, dedupe on meta.request_id), DynamoDB, Scheduler, S3 lifecycle and the open-source policy schema/evaluator with table tests. Target 80 h or less (estimate).

(6) State the following in the README and video:
- On TAKE devices, partner live view, clips and snapshots are encrypted during rollout, so the real-device path falls back to vehicle-event metadata plus helper confirmation in the native Ring app.
- Ring says support for the most recent 24 h of TAKE video is being worked on.
- Agency acceptance of rider-side records is unverified.

(7) Day-1 kill switches. Drop the concept if any of these holds:
- the Playground does not open for an India account;
- WHEP succeeds on fewer than 3 of 10 attempts with a browser offer sent after ICE gathering completes;
- a read of 10 more agency policies shows no written dispute or appeal path for a 'driver did not wait' claim.

(8) Demo, 45 s, in this order:
1. REAL: Playground live view on the helper's phone.
2. The helper taps 'Yes, that's my ride'.
3. The rider's tablet speaks 'Your ride is here; the driver waits until 2:12'.
4. The helper taps Accept.
5. SIMULATED (labelled) departure at 2 min 10 s.
6. The AVL review request is generated, quoting the clause and the deadline.

The solo 105 h estimate (estimate) is about 5.8 h/day over 18 working days once 2 recovery days are reserved. The MVP spans roughly 11 subsystems across browser CV, Python Lambdas, two PWAs with Web Push, PDF generation, an emulator harness and six AWS services, plus Firecrawl onboarding. That is too wide for one person; trimmed, it is roughly 80 h (estimate).

Day-1 unknowns:
(a) Whether the Playground opens for an India-based Amazon Developer account. This is unverified, and the console sits behind sign-in.
(b) What the Vehicle simulation shows. No entrant has published a Vehicle frame. The one Playground frame on record (doorstep-ring) is the package clip 'Thief stealing our package'. That entrant's vehicle scenario used an AI-generated driveway image, which suggests a usable Vehicle frame was not captured (inference).
(c) WHEP. This risk is lower than the concept states. DevRel in forum 45309 says a 500 is 'likely' caused by sending the offer before ICE gathering completes, and doorstep-ring got a 201 and 1280x720 frames with a headless-Chrome offer on 2026-09-23.

Structural problems for the real-device path:
- TAKE is the default for all customers worldwide once rolled out. Partner live view, clips and snapshots then return encrypted content, so the CV witness and evidence frames fail for most future households.
- The UX guide forbids analysing video inside privacy zones, and many owners mask the street.

name: QuietBell: a booking-aware silent doorbell for solo appointment pros
track: Ring (primary). Can also enter the AWS Builder and Open Source mini challenges.
pitch: For practitioners who have no front desk and are mid-service behind a closed door. A press on the shared Ring doorbell is matched to the right booking without identifying anyone. It is routed silently to that one practitioner's wrist or phone, and their one-tap acknowledgement appears on the client's booking link. If the client gives up and walks away before being seen, QuietBell flags it.
primary_user: Solo or small-suite appointment professionals who work behind a closed door with no receptionist and no staffed waiting room: salon-suite stylists, estheticians, massage therapists, tattoo artists, tutors and music teachers in a suite or home studio with a Ring doorbell at the entrance. The secondary user is the arriving client. Clinical practices covered by HIPAA are excluded from the MVP.
original_mechanism: Booking-aware routing of an arrival without identifying anyone. An assignment step scores every open ICS booking across the practitioners who share one door. The inputs are time offset from the start (an early/late band set per practice), whether that practitioner is in session now (from the calendar), party size from the CV person count compared with the booking's party size, and whether the booking is already matched. Clear wins go silently to one practitioner. Ambiguous ones go to both as 'maybe yours', and the first acknowledgement claims it. The practitioner's acknowledgement is pushed to the client's booking-link page (SSE), closing the loop the doorbell lacks. A walk-away check fires only on events: last motion.human end older than N minutes, then exactly one short confirmatory WHEP frame. That avoids continuous streaming and cluttering the owner's history. Output is a day log of observed arrival versus booked time, labelled as observations and never as attendance verdicts.
removal_test: This partly fails. Without Ring, a booking-link 'I'm here' button gives most of the routing and acknowledgement value, as TapIn and The Receptionist already show with iPads. Ring adds three things a link cannot: the press itself as check-in for clients who ignore links, the party size, and the walk-away signal. That is a real but narrow wedge, and it is the concept's main weakness. It fits best where there is no indoor waiting room and the door is the only touchpoint.
wow_moment_45s: 0-8 s: One door, two practitioners (Maya, Ravi), two bookings 3 minutes apart, both on a split screen of their phones. 8-20 s, REAL: Ring Playground live view (CC BY attribution on screen) feeds the in-browser person counter: 1 person in the door zone. SIMULATED (ring-sandbox, labelled): doorbell press at 2:57. Within about 2 s, only Maya's screen lights up with a silent 'Likely your 3:00, Jordan, party of 1, 3 min early'; Ravi's stays dark. 20-30 s: Maya taps 'Seen, about 5 min'. Jordan's booking link, open on a second phone, updates to say Maya knows they are here and will be about 5 minutes. 30-42 s, SIMULATED: no motion for 4 min, and a confirmatory frame of team footage counts 0 people. Maya gets 'Your 3:00 may have left (last seen 3:01), text them?' with a pre-filled message.

rivals.name: TapIn
rivals.our_difference: Needs no iPad or waiting room: the doorbell press is the check-in and works for clients who never open a link. Adds a party-size count and walk-away detection. Whether TapIn routes by booking time is not verified in reviewed sources.

rivals.name: The Receptionist / Sign In App
rivals.our_difference: Same acknowledgement loop, but triggered at a door with no iPad, matched to bookings, and with walk-away detection. Assumes an indoor lobby; QuietBell targets door-only setups.

rivals.name: Lobbywizard / I'm Here! notification systems
rivals.our_difference: No new hardware beyond an existing Ring doorbell. Matches to bookings rather than a name button, and detects walk-aways. The hardware rivals are simpler and fully offline.

rivals.name: Front Desk (hackathon entrant, banksythequantLab/front-desk)
rivals.our_difference: Front Desk classifies what is at the door (for example possible service of process). QuietBell matches the arrival to a booking, routes it to one practitioner, closes the acknowledgement loop to the client and detects walk-aways.

rivals.name: Lumeo (Ring Appstore)
rivals.our_difference: Analytics after the fact versus a per-booking routing and acknowledgement workflow. No demographics, deliberately.

mvp_scope: Playground token; device, status and configuration reads; privacy zones excluded from every frame analysis, and their coordinates never shown.
ICS import for 1-3 practitioners (Google Calendar ICS in the demo), with a booking-link page per appointment (accessible, live updates over SSE).
Matcher with scoring, an ambiguity threshold and the first-acknowledgement-claims protocol, with table-driven tests (early, late, overlapping bookings, party-size mismatch).
In-browser MediaPipe person counter on WHEP frames from the Playground Motion simulation (real), plus ring-sandbox snapshots of team footage (simulated).
ring-sandbox scenarios: shared_suite_rush, early_client, walk_away, link_only_client. button_press and motion_detected sub_type=human are delivered with HMAC.
Practitioner surface: a silent web-push card with Seen / N min / Not mine buttons. If unacknowledged, it escalates or sends an automatic estimate based on the calendar session end.

Walk-away check: last motion end plus one confirmatory frame. If the client left, a 'text them' button opens a pre-filled SMS from the practitioner's own phone, so no messaging infrastructure is needed.
AWS deployment, plus a README with a verified-vs-simulated table, a privacy notice template for the door sign, and a friction log.
hardware: MacBook M4 Pro for development. Three phones or browsers for two practitioners and one client in the demo. A smartphone to record consented doorway footage for simulated scenarios. No Ring hardware for the Playground path. Optional US-located Ring doorbell with a plan for the conditional real path.

estimate.cloud_cost_usd: Estimate: about $3-12 total through 20 Nov 2026. Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB and Scheduler stay within the listed free allowances at demo volume. CloudWatch and API Gateway cost a few dollars (API Gateway free-tier applicability on post-July-2025 accounts is unverified). No Bedrock or Rekognition calls; detection runs in the browser.
estimate.assumptions: Estimates, not measurements. One engineer. Hours include day-1 spikes (6h), Ring client and configuration handling (5h), WHEP sampler and person counter (12h), ICS import and matcher with tests (12h), emulator scenarios and webhook intake (7h), practitioner surface (9h), client booking page (7h), walk-away logic (6h), AWS deployment (8h), tests (5h), and docs, video and friction log (12h). hours_duo is elapsed hours per person with about 15% coordination overhead.

blockers: WHEP reliability on the Playground is contested between entrants.
No ding or human-motion events on the Playground; routing timing must be simulated and labelled.
Playground footage is not a practice doorway, so the CV demo is on whatever people appear in it plus team footage.
ICS export availability varies across booking tools (unverified).
iOS Web Push needs an installed PWA.
fallback: If confirmatory frames are unreliable: drop CV-based walk-away and send the client's booking page a 'still here?' check, using only motion end times. If judges' feedback or the falsification test shows the removal-test weakness is fatal: reposition as the door layer for shared suites, where one Ring doorbell replaces a doorbell that rings in every room. If WHEP fails: run the CV on emulator snapshots and keep real device and configuration reads.
judge_rejection_risks: The removal test is only partial: a link check-in like TapIn or The Receptionist delivers much of the value without Ring.
Demand evidence is mostly vendor marketing, and a Ring doorbell as a business check-in device is untested.
Close to the 'motion alert' Obvious category if the matching and acknowledgement loop are not front and centre.
Privacy of clients filmed at a business door, especially for wellness services. HIPAA practices are excluded, which narrows the market.
Most of the event layer is simulated for an India team.
Live-view sampling adds clutter to the owner's history and uses battery on battery-powered doorbells.
risk_profile: Low-medium technical risk (standard webhook, scheduling and CV pieces). Highest competition and substitution risk of the three (strong check-in rivals, partial removal test). Medium privacy risk (client footage at a business door). Low simulation risk relative to RNG-1, because routing logic is deterministic and testable.
aws_builder_path: API Gateway and a Lambda webhook receiver (HMAC on raw bytes, ack under 5 s), an SQS-buffered matcher Lambda, and DynamoDB (bookings, arrivals, claims, with TTL expiry). EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedules handle acknowledgement escalation and walk-away re-checks, so no long-running process is needed. Lambda serves the booking-link page and SSE stream (or API Gateway WebSocket; that pricing is not verified). Budgets alarm. Developed with Kiro or Claude Code on Bedrock. No model calls are needed in the decision path.
open_source_path: (1) Publish 'ics-arrival-matcher': a library that matches arrivals with no identity to ICS bookings, with explicit confidence, an ambiguity band and the first-acknowledgement-claims protocol, plus property-based tests. (2) Upstream ring-sandbox PR adding shared_suite_rush and walk_away scenarios. (3) A small 'whep-frame-sampler' utility for one-shot confirmatory frames from a Ring WHEP session, with documented failure modes.

name: OnAir: two-sided camera-use agreements for in-home workers
track: Ring (primary). Can also enter the AWS Builder and Open Source mini challenges.
pitch: A camera-use agreement that nannies, home-care aides or cleaners and the household that employs them both sign. It names which Ring cameras exist, when live view may be used and for what, and who sees what. During each shift the worker is told within moments when a Ring camera's live view is opened, whether that matched the agreement, and when camera privacy settings change. Both sides get a per-shift receipt. OnAir never stores or analyses video.
primary_user: Nannies, home-care aides and house cleaners working in homes that have Ring cameras; they are the people being filmed. Also the household employer who owns the Ring account, and optionally the agency that placed the worker. US focus, because of the Ring partner path.
original_mechanism: An inverted access log. During agreed shift windows only, a poller reads Event History for on_demand records and diffs device configurations and status against a versioned, two-party agreement. Sessions OnAir itself opened are attributed to the named viewer. All others are labelled 'Ring app or another app' (the API does not say who, and OnAir does not guess). A deterministic rule engine classifies each session as within agreement, outside agreement (time or purpose), or unexplained, and settings drift is detected the same way. Results go to the worker as low-key notices and to both parties as a per-shift receipt they each acknowledge. Changes to the agreement need both parties to accept again. The only media used is one field-of-view frame per camera at signing, shown and never stored (only its hash). OnAir's own media access can be checked through is_third_party_reviewed on every event.
removal_test: Without Ring nothing meaningful is left. The product is a transparency layer over Ring's own live-view and settings data. Ring is fully load-bearing. Caveat: the same pattern could later be extended to other camera vendors that expose access-log APIs, so the agreement schema is vendor-neutral.
wow_moment_45s: 0-10 s: The aide's phone, with no Ring account, shows today's agreement: Front Door camera, live view allowed for arrival checks, private hour 13:00-14:00, audio pledge, and a frame of what the camera sees (captured at signing). 10-25 s, REAL: on the household phone Dana taps 'Check the front door' in OnAir, which opens a real Playground WHEP session. The aide's phone shows 'Front Door live view opened 14:02 by Dana via OnAir, for an arrival check, which your agreement allows', then '47 s, within agreement' when it ends. The latency is measured on day 1 and shown on screen. 25-40 s, REAL event with a shifted demo clock that is labelled: a Playground console simulation creates an on_demand record not opened through OnAir. Both phones show 'Live view opened from the Ring app or another app during your private hour', and Dana is prompted to add a reason, which goes into the shared ledger. 40-45 s, SIMULATED (ring-sandbox fixture, labelled): Front Door privacy zones change from 2 to 0, and both sides are told 'Camera privacy setting changed'.

rivals.name: Attest (hackathon entrant, josepha-mayo/attest)
rivals.our_difference: Attest answers 'did the visit happen?' for disputes. OnAir answers 'how is the camera being used on me right now, and is that what we agreed?' for the person being filmed. Whether Attest notifies workers of live views opened in the Ring app is not verified in reviewed sources.

rivals.name: Ring app Event History (owner-side, native)
rivals.our_difference: Faces the worker and checks against the agreement. The filmed worker has no Ring account and sees nothing today.

rivals.name: Beside Care (Ring Appstore)
rivals.our_difference: Beside Care watches the person receiving care on the family's behalf. OnAir gives notice and an agreement to the worker who is being filmed. Worker-facing notices in Beside Care are not verified in reviewed sources.

rivals.name: Written nanny or agency work agreements (substitute)
rivals.our_difference: A paper agreement cannot tell the worker when a camera is actually viewed or when its settings change. OnAir makes the agreement observable.

mvp_scope: Agreement builder, filled from GET /v1/devices (user-assigned names, never IDs). Fields: allowed purposes, allowed and private windows, audio pledge, retention pledge, notice preferences. Both parties accept through magic links, and every version is kept.
Field-of-view preview at signing: one WHEP frame per camera, shown to both parties and then discarded, keeping only its hash.

Shift-window poller: on_demand history every 15 s per camera, filtered client-side (one entrant reports the event_types filter is ignored), with OnAir-opened sessions attributed to their named viewer.
Rule engine and configuration-drift detection (privacy-zone count, motion detection on/off, device offline), with unit tests on ring-sandbox fixtures.
Worker PWA: a status line ('camera live now' or 'last viewed'), low-key notices and the shift receipt. Household dashboard: notices delivered, breach reasons, and receipts both sides acknowledge.
Self-audit panel showing is_third_party_reviewed=false for every event, as proof OnAir never downloaded media.
Data deletion for either party, a privacy policy, and an explicit 'not legal advice' notice. AWS deployment.
hardware: MacBook M4 Pro for development. Two phones (household and worker). No Ring hardware for the Playground path. Optional US Ring Indoor Cam with a plan for the real path.

estimate.cloud_cost_usd: Estimate: about $2-8 total through 20 Nov 2026. Poller: 60 invocations/h over 8 h/day for 30 days is about 14,400 invocations; at about 50 s and 0.125 GB that is about 90,000 GB-s, roughly $1.50 at $0.0000166667/GB-s if outside the free allowance. DynamoDB and Scheduler cost cents, plus a few dollars of CloudWatch logs. No Bedrock, Rekognition or media storage.
estimate.assumptions: Estimates, not measurements. One engineer. Hours include day-1 spikes, including the latency measurement (6h), Ring client, poller and attribution (8h), agreement model with two-party acceptance and versioning (10h), rule engine and drift detection (7h), worker and household PWAs (14h), field-of-view preview (5h), AWS deployment (6h), tests on fixtures (5h), and docs, video and friction log (10h). hours_duo is elapsed hours per person with about 15% coordination overhead.

blockers: Unknown delay between a live view starting and its on_demand record appearing in history. Records may appear only after the session ends.
It is unverified whether live views opened in the owner's Ring app reach the partner history in practice; the doc says they do.
Reports conflict on the history event_types filter (an entrant says it is ignored; the forum says use the plural). Filter client-side.
The 30-min Playground token interrupts long demos.
Clear 'not legal advice' messaging is needed, so the product does not imply legal compliance.
fallback: If the delay is over 60 s or records only appear after a session ends: change the promise from 'live now' to 'notice within N minutes plus a per-shift receipt', and keep real-time notices for sessions opened through OnAir, which it knows about immediately. If Ring-app sessions do not appear: make the agreement require household live checks to go through OnAir's viewer (weaker, and stated honestly). If the employer-incentive test fails: reposition for agencies that place nannies and aides and would require it as a condition of placement.
judge_rejection_risks: Unclear buyer: why would an employer install a tool that reports on themselves? Adoption may depend on agencies or advocacy groups.
Can be read as a compliance dashboard with no 'wow' and no AI or CV. Tech Implementation may be judged thin unless the attribution, drift and latency engineering is shown.
It cannot say who opened a Ring-app live view, only that one happened.
Owner-app sessions are documented but cannot be demonstrated on the Playground.
Legal sensitivity: it must not suggest it makes a household compliant with recording or monitoring laws.
Niche user group in a hackathon whose Ring examples stress accessibility, caretaking and business.
risk_profile: Lowest technical and simulation risk of the three: the core loop runs on real Playground calls (devices, status, configurations, on_demand history, WHEP). Highest buyer-incentive risk. Medium legal and reputational sensitivity, which counts in its favour only if handled carefully. Lowest cloud cost.
aws_builder_path: EventBridge Scheduler (14M invocations/month free per the pricing page) triggers a 128 MB Lambda once a minute during shift windows; each invocation polls 4 times at 15 s intervals. DynamoDB stores agreements, sessions and receipts with TTL. Lambda sends Web Push. Optional KMS key to encrypt token material. Budgets alarm. Built with Kiro or Claude Code on Bedrock. Value: polling runs only while a worker is present (data minimisation) and costs close to nothing. No model is in the decision path.
open_source_path: (1) Publish a vendor-neutral 'camera-use-agreement' JSON schema with a reference rule engine and tests: windows, purposes, attribution classes, drift rules. It is useful to worker-advocacy groups and to other camera APIs. (2) Publish a 'ring-liveview-audit' library that turns on_demand history plus configuration diffs into a per-shift log, including the measured on_demand latency and the client-side event_types filtering workaround. (3) Upstream ring-sandbox PR adding a fidelity note or option for on_demand delay, based on measured Playground data.

conditions: OnAir-opened WHEP sessions produce on_demand records that GET history returns. Latency is measured over 20 trials and reported in the README.
Whether Playground console simulations also create on_demand records is verified. If not, a second labelled script stands in for 'another app'.
A 'not legal advice' notice. No claim of legal compliance. CC BY attribution for any Playground footage shown.
Both parties' consent screens are shown. The worker never handles Ring credentials.
gate.crowding_notes: josepha-mayo/attest (MIT, CI) logs the live-view sessions it brokers into signed coverage, which is the closest visible overlap; its answer is 'did the visit happen', not worker notice. The privacy, consent and redaction theme has about 19 visible repos across tracks (github.md), and AtchayamG/bee-bystander does consent for Bee.
gate.day_one_proof: With a Playground token: open 20 OnAir WHEP sessions and poll GET /v1/history/devices/{id}/events every 15 s. Each session must appear as an on_demand record; record the median and p90 latency, and whether records appear only after the session ends. Also read /configurations to confirm the privacy_zones and motion_detection fields are present for the drift diff.
gate.redesign_to_pass: Not required. To lift Tech Implementation, put the measured on_demand latency, the attribution classes and the drift diffing on screen, because the concept has no AI or CV 'wow'.

strongest_rival.rival: Attest (josepha-mayo/attest, Ring-track entrant, MIT, CI, also entering AWS Builder and Open Source)
strongest_rival.why: Attest serves the same people (in-home aides and households) on the same track with the same Ring mechanism. It polls Event History, keeps on_demand records as their own evidence kind, opens WHEP live views and writes each session (opened, closed, state) into signed coverage. Its README says 'Worker-facing pages show the same timeline the coordinator sees before they sign', so the worker already sees brokered live views after the visit. It has been built since 15 Sep and has KMS, signed packs, an offline verifier, an emulator and a signed live-API sweep. A Ring judge who sees both may read OnAir as an Attest feature turned around to face the worker. What Attest does not do, per its README: push notice to the worker during the shift, a two-party agreement on purposes, windows and a private hour, rule classification of each session, or configuration-drift notices. Whether Attest's worker view includes live views opened in the Ring app (as opposed to ones it brokered) is not stated (inference: probably not surfaced as notice).

redteam_round1.differentiation_holds:
Partly. It is narrower than the concept claims.

Against native Ring:
- No native notice reaches the person being filmed. BGR: 'Ring does not officially state that any light means someone is actively watching'. The Indoor Cam light table lists 'recording', with no live-view-specific pattern.
- Event history is owner-side only.
- Native Modes can switch off Live View and Recording per camera for Disarmed, Home and Away (Ring support). The household can therefore already enforce a private hour natively. But Modes are not in the Partner API, OnAir cannot check them, and the worker gets no proof.
- Privacy Zones (up to two per device) exist natively. Only their count is readable, which supports the drift beat.

Against substitutes:
- Contract camera clauses with 'a dated acknowledgment' for each new camera, room or audio change are already standard practice (Beverly).
- The versioned agreement therefore copies a free norm. Only the runtime observation (session records checked against the agreement, plus drift) is new.

Against rivals:
- Attest shows brokered live views to the worker after the visit, but not as in-shift notice against an agreement.
- My limited search found no worker-facing product that alerts the person being filmed (low confidence: absence of evidence).
- Beside Care faces the care recipient.

The differentiation survives only if the pitch centres on 'Ring's own session records, checked against what both sides signed' and is framed as complementary to Attest ('Attest proves the visit happened; OnAir shows the camera was used as agreed'). As a 'compliance dashboard' it collapses into a contract clause.
redteam_round1.redesign:
Make it 'OnAir: a metadata-only camera-use receipt', with the household announcing a check and Ring's record confirming it.

1. OnAir never touches media. Remove the brokered WHEP viewer and the production field-of-view frame.
   - The self-audit becomes true and checkable: OnAir only calls devices, status, configurations and history, so is_third_party_reviewed should stay false (verify on day 1).
   - It also works on TAKE devices, where video-reading partner apps get encrypted content (FAQ Q10). That is a Ring-specific, judge-legible advantage.
   - Camera coverage at signing comes from the device names plus household-written placement notes (room type, what is in view, audio on or off as a pledge). A Playground WHEP frame may appear only in the demo, clearly labelled, and opened by the stand-in tool below, not by OnAir.

2. Announce, then match, instead of attribution through OnAir's own viewer.
   - Before checking, the household taps 'I'm checking the front door: arrival check'. The worker gets that announcement at once; it is honestly real-time because it is a declaration.
   - When Ring's history later shows the on_demand record, OnAir matches it to the announcement. Classes:
     - announced and confirmed by Ring
     - announced, no record seen
     - unannounced (prompts a reason, logged in the ledger)
     - outside the agreed window or purpose
   - This turns the staged app-to-app beat into a check of the human's claim against Ring's own record.

3. The demo uses a separate, labelled 'Ring-app stand-in' tool: a browser WHEP session plus the Playground console buttons. It creates the on_demand records the poller finds, with a real wall-clock overlay. The promise becomes 'notice after the session, median N s measured over 20 trials', not 'within moments'.

4. Honest exposure in the receipt:
   - Add 'camera recorded N motion events during your shift' (production; fixture-labelled on the Playground).
   - Add a fixed line: 'OnAir cannot see playback of recorded clips or audio use.' This removes the false-reassurance problem.

5. Frame the camera honestly. The Playground doorbell is the 'arrival and door' camera. Indoor cameras are the production path. The agreement includes a private-quarters exclusion checklist (Virginia rule per Fi2W; Washington HB 2355 per a vendor blog, unverified against official text).

6. Position the product as complementary to Attest. Target placement agencies as the channel, since a household choosing it alone is the weak link.

7. Day-1 kill tests:
   - (a) A console button press and a browser WHEP session each yield an on_demand record within 5 min. If not, kill the concept.
   - (b) is_third_party_reviewed stays false when only metadata is called.
   - (c) Playground /configurations returns image_enhancements.privacy_zones and motion_detection.enabled.

8. Cut from the MVP: OnAir's own viewer and the field-of-view hashing. This saves about 8-10 h (estimate), to spend on latency instrumentation, the token-paste and replay modes for judges, and household-side access logs of OnAir's own calls (Content Policy §1.2.2).

Even with this redesign it remains a modest-scoring, low-risk entry. It fixes the contradictions, but not the buyer-incentive problem or the absence of a 'wow'.
redteam_round1.feasibility_attack:
The 70 h solo estimate is plausible (estimate). The risks sit in the platform, not in the hours.

1. WHEP on the Playground is contested.
   - doorstep-ring got a frame on 23 Sep, but 'Only an offer built by headless Chrome works'.
   - Attest's signed sweep on 30 Sep lists WHEP as a fail: 'needs streaming hardware on the account'.
   - The field-of-view frame and the 'Check the front door' beat both depend on WHEP. Use a browser WebRTC offer (the ring-api-helloworld Next.js path), never a server-side client.

2. In production, TAKE removes video for partners. FAQ Q10 says a TAKE device stays callable, but 'video requests return encrypted content, so your app cannot read recordings or snapshots, or open a live stream'. TAKE is rolling out as the default from September 2026, so the brokered viewer and the field-of-view frame would fail for most real users. The metadata core (history, configurations, status) should keep working (inference from 'visible and callable'). E2EE devices drop out of the API entirely.

3. The self-audit contradicts itself.
   - is_third_party_reviewed is defined as 'whether your partner app has previously downloaded media (video or image) for this event'.
   - OnAir opens WHEP sessions itself, so the panel's promise ('OnAir never pulled media') is false by construction.
   - Whether WHEP flips the flag is unknown. Attest also reports that its own snapshot media requests create on_demand records.

4. Attribution can only be by time-matching. The organizer (45309) confirms history attributes are exactly event_type, is_third_party_reviewed, start and end, so nothing says who opened a session. A Ring-app session that overlaps OnAir's own session will be misattributed.

5. The event_types filter is ignored. Attest reports this, and the forum poster saw singular forms ignored. Filter client-side.

6. Latency is unmeasured. Records carry start and end, so they may appear only after a session ends. Partner sessions cap at 60 s, but Ring-app Extended Live View runs up to 30 min, which means notice could come up to 30 min late. 'Within moments' is an overclaim.

7. Judges cannot exercise the deployed PWA without their own 30-minute Playground token. Ship a 'paste your Playground token' mode and a labelled replay mode, or the live URL will show an expired state through 20 Nov.

8. The central promise cannot be verified from India: catching live views opened in the owner's Ring app needs US hardware, a plan and account linking. It rests only on the doc line 'User or partner initiated a live view session'.

None of these is a hard blocker. Items 1-3 require dropping media from OnAir's own path.
redteam_round1.demo_attack:
Beat 10-25 s, 'REAL' (Dana taps Check the front door; the aide's phone shows the notice instantly):
- The instant notice is OnAir's own app sending a message to its other app. It comes from the button tap, not from Ring data.
- The Ring contribution is just a WHEP stream, which is itself contested on the Playground.
- A sharp judge sees 'app A pushes to app B', which is a staged wow.

Beat 25-40 s, a console simulation shown as a live view from the Ring app or another app:
- This is the only beat that really comes from Ring data. The organizer confirms that the Package, Vehicle and Motion buttons write on_demand records, so the record is genuine.
- But in the console it is a 'Motion' button press, presented as a Ring-app live view, with a shifted demo clock. It is credible only if the stand-in is labelled on screen and a real wall-clock timer shows the actual poll-to-notice delay. A hard cut would hide that delay and make the beat look faked.

Beat 40-45 s: a fixture. Labelled and honest, but simulated.

Net: one of the three beats is real Ring-derived behaviour. The headline value (catching Ring-app live views) is only ever shown by a stand-in.

Story problems:
- The Playground device is an outdoor doorbell. A 'private hour 13:00-14:00' on a porch camera does not convince anyone, because worker privacy fears centre on indoor cameras and audio (Fi2W; Beverly).
- False reassurance: Beverly says families mostly use disclosed footage for after-the-fact checks such as 'confirming the 12:30 nap actually happened'. Reviewing recorded clips does not create on_demand records (inference: they are not live views). A worker who sees '0 live views today' may wrongly believe nobody watched. That is a design and ethics flaw a Ring privacy judge could raise.
- There is no AI or CV moment. Tech Implementation will be scored on how well the API is used, against Attest and nightlight, which look heavier.
redteam_round1.eligibility_attack:
No hard blocker.

What passes:
- The Rules (section 4, Ring) accept 'Any Ring API, SDK, simulator, or device listed in Ring's developer documentation'. The video must show the project 'working through a simulator or an actual Ring device'. The Playground is in Ring's release notes, and the FAQ names it as a simulator.
- The runtime hook is met by server-side calls to api.amazonvision.com.
- Organizer forum 45309 confirms the Playground is 'the only documented route that needs neither a US device nor an account link'.

Caveats:
1. ring-sandbox is not 'listed in Ring's developer documentation'. It can only support labelled side beats, such as the drift fixture, never the core loop.
2. The concept cites 'Content Policy §12.2'. The clause is §1.2.2. It also says 'Apps must provide to Ring customers easy access to monitoring activity or access logs'. That duty is owed to the Ring customer (the household), about the app's own access. OnAir therefore also needs a household-facing log of its own API calls. Its claim to 'match Ring's direction' is an inference, not policy text.
3. §4.1.1 makes employers responsible for notice and consents. OnAir must not imply it discharges that duty. Keep the 'not legal advice' notice, and make no compliance claims about Connecticut, Washington or any other state.
4. Sharing the account holder's live-view activity with a third party (the worker) needs the account holder's explicit, affirmative consent. The two-party signing covers this; show it on screen.
5. Video rules: credit the CC BY Playground footage on screen if any frame appears. Show no third-party brands or logos, such as nanny agencies or other camera vendors.
6. Not a latent-LLM idea: there is no model in the decision path, and it is not an existing Ring feature (see differentiation).
